vignette:
Kwame Asante is a twenty-year-old Ghanaian-American man who, by any conventional measure, had achieved something extraordinary: he had completed an accelerated pre-medical track and entered a dual-degree programme that placed him, at nineteen, in a field medicine rotation embedded with a humanitarian surgical unit operating near an active conflict zone in West Africa. He had gone believing, with the particular certainty of the very young and very gifted, that medicine was a moral technology - that if you were skilled enough and present enough, you could hold the line between life and death. What happened in the third week of that rotation dismantled that belief so completely that he is now, seven months later, sitting across from a therapist in a university counselling centre, unable to articulate who he is or what he thought he knew.

The incident occurred during what had been described as a secured perimeter. A convoy carrying wounded civilians arrived at the field unit, and Kwame was assisting in triage when the compound came under direct fire. The assault was brief - accounts suggest under four minutes - but within that window he witnessed close-range violence of a kind that no training had approximated. He was pressed against an interior wall when the shooting stopped, and what followed was a silence so absolute it felt like a physical substance filling the room. In that silence he became aware that he could not catch his breath, that his chest had locked, that the air around him seemed to have been evacuated. The medic beside him was dead. The silence lasted perhaps thirty seconds before voices returned. Kwame did not move for considerably longer than that.

In the months since his return to the United States, the memory of that event has not cohered into anything he can hold steadily. He describes it in session as arriving in shards - a boot, a particular quality of light, the weight of a piece of equipment he cannot place - and when he tries to press further into the sequence, something intervenes before the picture completes. There are stretches he cannot recover at all, regardless of effort, and the pieces that do surface do not connect into a narrative that makes sense to him. He does not experience this as relief. He experiences it as a kind of structural damage, as though the event has left a hole in his cognition he keeps falling into.

What frightens Kwame most in his daily life is how little warning his body gives him. He is now in his first year of medical school proper, and the clinical environment has become a landscape of ambush. When he is moving quickly through a corridor and his breathing tightens from exertion, the sensation is enough to return him, partially, to the wall. When a simulation room goes quiet between instructions, the silence lands on him like a weight. He has watched a training video depicting surgical complications that included footage of physical violence and sat rigid at his desk for the remainder of the afternoon, unable to account for the time. His performance in small-group sessions has deteriorated, and one faculty supervisor has noted that he appears "elsewhere" during clinical skills practice.

He has come to believe that the world does not operate according to the principles he organised his life around - that competence is not protection, that presence does not guarantee outcome, that the moral logic he built his ambition on was a story he told himself in the absence of evidence. He no longer recognises the person who boarded the flight to that assignment. He is certain that remaining alert to threat at all times is not paranoia but the only rational response to what he now understands the world to actually be.

What finally brought him to seek help was a practical crisis: he missed a required assessment after sitting outside the examination room for forty minutes, unable to enter because he could hear, through the closed door, complete silence. He told the programme coordinator he had been unwell. He told the counsellor, in their first session, that he was afraid he had made a catastrophic error in choosing medicine - and then, more quietly, that he was afraid there was no longer enough of himself left to make any choice at all.
